---
title: "Definitions and Intuitions"
subtitle: "Étale morphisms through small examples"
---

## Definition

A morphism $f\colon X\to Y$ between schemes is **étale** if it is

1. locally of finite presentation,
2. flat, and
3. unramified.

::: {.callout-tip title="Intuition"}
We could think of an étale map as a map that is locally an isomorphism. It can be rigorously proven for varieties.
:::

## Example: an open immersion

Every open immersion \(U\hookrightarrow X\) is étale. Nothing changes near a
point of \(U\): we have only restricted our attention to a smaller open set.

## Example: the power map

Assume that \(n\) is invertible in the base field. On the punctured affine
line, the map

$$
\mathbb G_m \longrightarrow \mathbb G_m, \qquad t\longmapsto t^n
$$

is étale. Infinitesimally its derivative is \(nt^{n-1}\), which never vanishes
on \(\mathbb G_m\).

::: {.callout-warning title="Where the picture breaks"}
On the whole affine line, \(t\mapsto t^n\) ramifies at \(t=0\). The map is no
longer étale there: the branches collide.
:::

## What to remember

- Open immersions are the simplest étale maps.
- Étale maps may have several sheets, but they have no infinitesimal branching.
